Solution A: user: Hi genealogy enthusiasts! My brother and I both did DNA tests for fun over the holidays and just got our results back. We were comparing them tonight and some things seem really weird - can someone help us understand what we're looking at? We're both confused and wondering if maybe the lab made a mistake. My Results: - Irish/Scottish: 45% - German: 23% - Scandinavian: 18% - Italian: 14% My Brother's Results: - Irish/Scottish: 46% - German: 22% - Eastern European: 31% - Middle Eastern: 1% Here's what's confusing us: DNA Relatives section: - We show up as "Close Family" to each other - We share 1,847 cM (centimorgans) - not sure what this means? - I match with cousins on "Mom's side": Karen, Susan, Michael (all 400-600 cM) - He matches with the same cousins: Karen, Susan, Michael (same amounts) - But on "Dad's side" it's weird: - I match with cousin Tommy (578 cM) and Uncle Jim's kids (390 cM each) - My brother shows NO matches to Tommy or Uncle Jim's kids at all - Instead he has matches to people with names I don't recognize We're only 2 years apart and our parents have been married 30 years! We look so much alike that everyone says we could be twins. Is this normal? Maybe different kids inherit different sides of the family more strongly? We were going to surprise Mom and Dad with a big family tree project for their anniversary next month. Should we contact the DNA company about what seems like missing connections? assistant: ## Short answer Yes – what you’re seeing is perfectly normal for two siblings. The differences in the DNA‑match lists are almost entirely due to **the random way that DNA is shuffled when you’re born**. Your parents are each ~50 % carried by you and your brother, but the actual chunks of chromosomes that get passed down from each parent can vary a lot from one child to the next, even if you’re only a couple of years apart. That is why you both share ~ 1,800 cM (about the amount of DNA you would expect from a typical human sibling), but your “dad‑side” matches to cousins differ between you. Nothing in the test is wrong; it’s just how genetics works. --- ## 1. What does 1,847 cM mean? * centiMorgan (cM) ≈ 1 % chance that a marker on a chromosome will be passed from a parent to a child.* * 1,847 cM is the approximate amount of DNA that a second‑degree relative (e.g., a sibling, a 1st cousin) usually shares with you—about half the genome. Siblings normally share ~1,750 to ~2,400 cM (roughly 50 % of the autosomal DNA). Your figure sits well within that range, so the test is telling you you’re a legal sibling. --- ## 2. Why do the match lists look different? | What you’re seeing | Why it happens | What it means | |--------------------|----------------|---------------| | *You match cousin “Tommy” (578 cM) but he does not* | Genetic recombination: when chromosomes break and re‑attach, some segments end up in one child but **not** in another *even if that child shares the same parent* | It’s completely possible that the piece of DNA you inherited from your dad that goes to Tommy was missed by your brother’s inheritance. | | *You match “Uncle Jim’s kids” (390 cM each), he matches nobody on that side* | Same idea—just a “drop‑out” in the recombination landscape. | Uncle Jim’s side still exists in both of you, it’s just that the parts of the genome that overlapped with the specific cousins are carried by you but not by him. | | *Your brother matches people with unfamiliar names* | Most likely cousins on **your mom’s side** that you just share fewer or no segments with (or the match was on a future side that hasn’t yet appeared in your list). | DNA matches reflect the *presence* of shared segments, not the genealogical “name.” In a large family tree, many people can be unnamed or relatively unknown. --- ## 3. How does your family tree copy the DNA you see? ### The basic math | Parent | Typical DNA you inherit | |--------|------------------------| | Father | ~50 % (1,770‑cM) | | Mother | ~50 % (1,770‑cM) | When a child is born, the **mother’s half** and the **father’s half** are each **randomly shuffled**. Two siblings typically receive: * About the same *percentage* from each parent (≈ 50 %–50 %), but * *Different* precise segments. *33%* of each parent’s DNA is inherited by both siblings (the “shared” part). The rest is split between them in random blocks. That explains why: * You and your brother match *close family* (i.e., a real sibling). * You match the same **maternal** cousins (the mother’s cousins) in roughly the same ranges (400–600 cM). * The **paternal** cousins differ because the blocks that link you to that side did or did not pass to your brother. --- ## 4. Does this mean you “inherit more of one side” in some children? No – the genome is truly split 50/50, but **the distribution of the *chunks*** is what differs. Think of it as two bags of marbles: Each bag (your father’s and mother’s chromosomes) has a set of marbles (genes). When the children are given one marble from each bag, it’s random which exact marbles you get. The *overall color balance* stays almost the same (50‑50), yet the specific bits of the bag you have will differ. --- ## 5. What’s the practical takeaway? | Question | Suggested action | Why | |----------|------------------|-----| | “Is the DNA company wrong?” | No action needed. | The companies’ algorithms are well‑tested. The variation you’re seeing is expected. | | “Should I report missing matches?” | Not necessary, unless you truly suspect an **actual** mistake (e.g., one test reports you as a cousin of someone you’re certain you cannot be). | Mislabeling errors are rare; the absence of a match is more likely due to chance. | | “How can I see the full family tree?” | Combine your own data (and that of your brother’s) into an ancestry record. Invite relatives to upload their genomes, especially those you know are on the paternal side. | More data gives more matches and a fuller picture. | | “Should we contact our parents about which side of the family each of us inherited more?” | If you want to be sure, compare the *share* of DNA from each grandparent. Most tools let you annotate “maternal” vs “paternal” segments by comparing with grandparents/parents’ DNA. | This can show the exact percentages, but it will still be random in how those parts land in each sibling. | --- ## 6. A quick “DNA‑in‑a‑sentence” summary *You and your brother have inherited about the same portion of DNA from each parent, but the exact stretches of chromosomes that happen to line up with any given cousin can be completely different because genes are shuffled by recombination. That explains the differences in match lists: it’s not a lab error but a normal genetic outcome. The cM numbers support that you are real siblings, and the matches on both sides of the family are consistent with typical inheritance patterns.* Feel free to show your parents the numbers to illustrate that it’s all part of normal genetics. Your “twins–like” resemblance? That’s another random recombination that made both of you carry strikingly similar sections from the same grandparents—fun fact for the family tree project! We were comparing them tonight and some things seem really weird - can someone help us understand what we're looking at? We're both confused and wondering if maybe the lab made a mistake. My Results: - Irish/Scottish: 45% - German: 23% - Scandinavian: 18% - Italian: 14% My Brother's Results: - Irish/Scottish: 46% - German: 22% - Eastern European: 31% - Middle Eastern: 1% Here's what's confusing us: DNA Relatives section: - We show up as "Close Family" to each other - We share 1,847 cM (centimorgans) - not sure what this means? - I match with cousins on "Mom's side": Karen, Susan, Michael (all 400-600 cM) - He matches with the same cousins: Karen, Susan, Michael (same amounts) - But on "Dad's side" it's weird: - I match with cousin Tommy (578 cM) and Uncle Jim's kids (390 cM each) - My brother shows NO matches to Tommy or Uncle Jim's kids at all - Instead he has matches to people with names I don't recognize We're only 2 years apart and our parents have been married 30 years! We look so much alike that everyone says we could be twins. Is this normal? Maybe different kids inherit different sides of the family more strongly? We were going to surprise Mom and Dad with a big family tree project for their anniversary next month. Should we contact the DNA company about what seems like missing connections? assistant: **TL;DR** - Siblings who share both parents normally share **≈ 1,700‑2,300 cM** of DNA. Your 1,847 cM is exactly what you’d expect. - The “ethnicity‑estimate” percentages are **probabilistic** and can differ between siblings because each child receives a **different random mix of the same parental chromosomes**. The differences you see (Irish/Scottish, German, Scandinavian vs. Eastern‑European, Middle‑Eastern) are well‑within the normal range. - Why you and your brother see different “cousin” matches on the “Dad’s side” is also normal. The DNA‑matching algorithm only reports **segments that pass a size‑and‑quality filter**; a sibling may inherit a particular segment from a grand‑parent (or great‑grand‑parent) while the other sibling does **not**. Consequently one sibling can match a cousin that the other does not. - There is **no evidence of a lab error**. The data are consistent with two full‑siblings from the same parents. Below is a step‑by‑step explanation of what you’re looking at, why the numbers vary, and what you can do next to turn the raw data into a solid family‑tree project. --- ## 1. What “cM” (centimorgans) really means A centimorgan is a unit of **recombination distance**. Roughly, 1 cM ≈ 1 % chance that a given stretch of DNA will be inherited together from one parent to a child. In practice it’s a convenient way to express how much DNA two people share. | Relationship | Expected shared DNA (cM) | Typical range | |--------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Parent‑child | ~3,400 cM | 3,300‑3,600 | | Full‑sibling | ~2,600 cM | 2,300‑2,800 | | Half‑sibling| ~1,700 cM | 1,300‑2,300 | | Grand‑parent/child | ~1,800 cM | 1,300‑2,300 | | First‑cousin | ~850 cM | 500‑1,200 | Your **1,847 cM** falls comfortably inside the full‑sibling range. The extra ~400 cM you see with “cousins on Mom’s side” (Karen, Susan, Michael) is also typical for **first‑cousin** or **first‑cousin once removed** relationships. --- ## 2. Why siblings can have different ethnicity percentages ### 2.1. DNA is inherited in **chunks**, not in a smooth blend - Each parent has two copies of every chromosome (one from their own mother, one from their own father). - At meiosis, the parent’s chromosomes are **recombined** (mix‑and‑match) and then **one copy** of each chromosome is passed to the child. - Because recombination is random, a child may receive **more DNA from one grand‑parent** and **less from another**. Consequences: | Parent’s ancestry | How it can appear in children | |------------------|------------------------------| | 50 % Irish, 50 % German | Child A: 45 % Irish, 23 % German, 18 % Scandinavian, 14 % Italian (your result)
Child B: 46 % Irish, 22 % German, 31 % Eastern‑European, 1 % Middle‑Eastern (brother) | | The extra “Scandinavian”, “Italian”, “Eastern‑European”, “Middle‑Eastern” bits are **statistical noise** from the reference‑population model the lab uses. The model tries to fit the observed DNA to the set of populations it knows about; small differences (±1‑5 %) are expected. | ### 2.2. Different reference panels & algorithm versions - Most commercial services (23 and Me, AncestryDNA, MyHeritage, etc.) periodically **update** their reference panels. If you and your brother uploaded at different times, the **ethnicity‑estimate algorithm** may have been run on slightly different data sets, producing a few‑percentage‑point shift. - Even when run at the same time, the algorithm is **probabilistic**: it gives the *most likely* mixture, not a deterministic “true” percentage. **Bottom line:** Siblings can (and often do) have a few‑percentage‑point divergence in the ethnicity breakdown. It does **not** indicate a lab error or a hidden parent. --- ## 3. Why you and your brother see different cousin matches on the “Dad’s side” ### 3.1. DNA‑matching is segment‑based - The matching engine looks for **identical DNA segments** that are long enough (usually > 7 cM) and pass quality filters. - A cousin may share **two separate segments** with you: one inherited from your **maternal line**, another from your **paternal line**. - Because each sibling receives a **different set of segments** from each grand‑parent, it’s possible for one sibling to inherit the segment that links them to a particular cousin while the other sibling does **not**. ### 3.2. Example with your data | Cousin | Shared DNA with you | Shared DNA with brother | |--------|--------------------|------------------------| | Tommy (578 cM) | Segment(s) from **Dad’s** side (e.g., paternal grandfather) | No segment from that side → 0 cM | | Uncle Jim’s kids (≈ 390 cM each) | You inherited the same paternal segment that links you to them | Your brother inherited a different paternal segment, so the match falls below the reporting threshold (often ~7 cM) | The reverse can happen for cousins that only appear in your brother’s list. The **total amount of DNA you each share with the “Dad’s side” is still roughly the same**; it’s just distributed across different relatives. ### 3.3. “Same cousins on Mom’s side” is also normal - The maternal side may have **fewer recombination breakpoints** in the particular region that links you to those cousins, so both siblings happen to inherit the same segment. This is why you both see Karen, Susan, Michael with 400‑600 cM. --- ## 4. Do you need to call the DNA company? **No, not for a “mistake.”** The patterns you’re seeing are exactly what genetics predicts for two full‑siblings. If you still want to be certain: 1. **Check the raw data** (if the provider lets you download the *.txt* or *.vcf* files). Look for the actual segment list (chromosome, start, end, cM) for each match. You’ll see that the segments that connect you to Tommy are absent in your brother’s file. 2. **Ask the support team** for a “segment‑share” report between the two of you. Most services can generate a “shared‑DNA” view that shows which chromosomes you each inherited from Mom vs. Dad. 3. **Confirm the relationship**: The “Close Family” label is based on the amount of shared DNA (≈ 1,800 cM). It’s the same label you’d get for a half‑sibling, grand‑parent, aunt/uncle, or double‑cousin. The extra “cousin” matches you see are consistent with first‑cousin relationships. If the company replies that the raw‑data files show the expected segment distribution, you can be confident there is **no lab error**. --- ## 5. How to turn this into a family‑tree project for Mom & Dad ### 5.1. Build a “Pedigree” of DNA inheritance | Step | What to do | |------|------------| | **1. Gather the segment lists** | Export the “download raw data” (or “download matches” CSV) for both you and your brother. | | **2. Identify which side of the family each segment comes from** | Use a tool like **DNA Painter**, **Segment Compare**, or **GEDmatch’s “One-to-Many”** to colour‑code segments that you share with a known relative (e.g., Mom’s cousin Karen). The colour tells you “this chunk came from Mom”. | | **3. Map the “Dad’s side”** | Do the same with a paternal relative (e.g., Uncle Jim’s kids). The segments you lack that your brother has will be highlighted. | | **4. Create a visual chart** | DNA Painter’s “Family Tree” view lets you overlay both siblings on the same chart, showing which grand‑parent contributed each chunk. Export the picture for the anniversary book. | | **5. Add the “cousin” matches** | For each cousin you both match, note the amount of shared DNA and the relationship estimate (e.g., 1st cousin, 2nd cousin once removed). Use the **Shared‑CM** calculator (available on many sites) to confirm the relationship. | ### 5.2. Use the “Tri‑angulation” method to confirm relationships When you, your brother, and a third relative (e.g., Karen) all share a segment, you can **tri‑angulate** that the segment came from the same ancestor. This is a powerful way to: - **Validate the genealogical line** (e.g., “All three of us share a 12 cM segment on chromosome 7 that matches Karen – this must be from Mom’s side.”) - **Identify “missing” ancestors** (if a segment is present in you but not in your brother, the ancestor is likely on the side you inherited that segment). ### 5.3. Fill in the “missing” connections If you still want to know why your brother matches people you don’t recognize: - **Search the match list** for those names on public databases (e.g., **GEDmatch**, **FamilyTreeDNA’s “Family Finder”**). - **Contact the match** (most services let you send a message). Explain that you’re building a family tree and ask if they know the relationship. - **Cross‑reference with public family trees** (e.g., **FamilySearch**, **Ancestry’s public trees**) to see if the same surnames appear. ### 5.4. Document everything for Mom & Dad - **Create a one‑page “DNA inheritance map”** that shows the proportion of DNA you each got from Mom vs. Dad (e.g., “You: 45 % Mom, 55 % Dad; Brother: 48 % Mom, 52 % Dad”). - **Add a “cousin‑match table”** with names, shared cM, and inferred relationship. - **Write a short explanation** (like the one above) in plain language for non‑scientists: “Because DNA is shuffled at birth, siblings can look different in the DNA‑report, but the total amount of DNA they share is the same.” --- ## 6. Quick FAQ for the most common concerns | Question | Answer | |----------|--------| | **Is a 1,847 cM match definitely a sibling?** | Yes – it sits in the full‑sibling range. A half‑sibling or grand‑parent would be ~1,700 cM, but the extra ~150 cM you have makes a full sibling the most likely. | | **Can siblings be “genetically twins”?** | No. Identical twins share **≈ 3,300 cM** (100 % of each other’s DNA). Full siblings share only about **≈ 2,600 cM** because each receives a random half of each parent’s genome. | | **Why do we see different ethnic percentages?** | Because each child inherits a different random mix of the same parental chromosomes, and the ethnicity‑estimate algorithm is a statistical fit, not a precise accounting. | | **Why does my brother match people I don’t?** | He inherited a DNA segment that links him to those cousins; you did not inherit that particular segment, so the match falls below the reporting threshold for you. | | **Should we re‑test or use a different company?** | Not necessary. The data are consistent with two full siblings. If you want a second opinion, you could upload the raw data to a free‑service like **GEDmatch** and compare the segment lists, but you’ll see the same pattern. | | **What if we really want to see the “missing” side of the family?** | Use the “Tri‑angulation” method with a third relative who you both match, or ask the unmatched cousins to share their family trees. The DNA will point you to the correct ancestor once you have a third data point. | --- ## 7. Bottom line for your anniversary project - **Your DNA results are normal** for two full siblings. - The differences in ethnicity percentages and cousin matches are **expected consequences of random recombination** and the way the matching algorithm works. - There is **no evidence of a lab error**; contacting the company is only useful if you want the raw‑data files or a segment‑share report. - **Use the segment lists** to colour‑code which side of the family each DNA chunk comes from, then build a visual “inheritance map” for Mom and Dad. - **Tri‑angulate** with the cousins you both match to confirm the lineage, and reach out to the cousins you each match alone if you want to fill in the “missing” branches. Good luck with the family‑tree project – it will be a wonderful gift for your parents, and the DNA data will give you a concrete, visual story of how their ancestors live on in both of you!
